mcqs.question: An x86 addressing mode computes `base + index*scale + offset` inside a single load instruction. Why does this matter for instruction selection?
options: It means the IR itself must be rewritten to use x86-specific syntax
It has no effect on generated code, since all instructions execute in the same number of cycles regardless
It only matters for floating-point operations, not integer address computation
A well-matched instruction selector can fuse several IR-level add/multiply steps into that one instruction instead of emitting each separately, which is a real, measurable performance difference
mcqs.explanation: Recognizing that a whole chunk of IR maps to one fused hardware instruction instead of several separate ones is exactly the pattern-matching job of instruction selection, and missing that fusion produces correct but slower code. The IR stays target-neutral regardless of what any one target supports, instructions don't all cost the same, and this addressing-mode fusion applies to ordinary integer address computation, not specifically floats.

mcqs.question: Two virtual registers, A and B, have live ranges that never overlap in time. What does this let register allocation do?
options: Delete one of the two registers entirely from the IR
Merge A and B's values into a single virtual register before allocation begins
Safely assign both A and B to the same physical register, since they're never simultaneously needed
Force both to be spilled to memory regardless of register availability
mcqs.explanation: Non-overlapping live ranges mean A and B are never both needed at the same instant, so reusing one physical register for both is completely safe and is exactly the reasoning that lets a CPU's small register set serve far more virtual values than it has slots for. This isn't about deleting or merging registers in the IR itself, and it doesn't force spilling — quite the opposite, it avoids the need for it.

mcqs.question: Why do most real compilers use heuristics for register allocation instead of computing a provably optimal graph coloring?
options: Graph coloring is NP-hard in general, so an exact solver doesn't scale, and heuristics trade some allocation quality for practical, bounded compile times
Optimal coloring would require rewriting the source program
Physical registers don't actually need to be assigned correctly, only approximately
Heuristics are used only for floating-point register allocation, never integer
mcqs.explanation: Exact graph coloring is NP-hard, so a compiler (especially a JIT compiling while a program is already running) can't afford to search for a provably optimal solution — heuristics like Chaitin-style coloring or linear scan trade some allocation quality for compile-time speed that actually fits within a real build or JIT budget. This has nothing to do with rewriting source code, correctness is still required (not approximate), and the same heuristic approach applies to both integer and floating-point registers.

mcqs.question: A function has more simultaneously-live values than the target has physical registers. What does the allocator do, and what does it cost?
options: It refuses to compile the function until the source code is rewritten
It silently drops the least recently used value from the program
It automatically increases the number of physical registers available at runtime
It spills one or more values to memory, paying a memory access on every use of the spilled value instead of a near-free register read
mcqs.explanation: Spilling stores the value to the stack and reloads/stores it around each use — a real, measurable cost (tens of cycles for memory versus roughly one for a register) rather than a compile failure. The compiler doesn't refuse to build, doesn't silently drop program values, and physical register count is a fixed hardware property that can't be changed at runtime.

mcqs.question: Why does an incorrect calling convention implementation tend to produce bugs that show up far from the actual mistake?
options: Because the calling convention is the only shared contract at a function-call boundary — corrupting a register the convention promises is preserved shows up wherever that register is next read, not at the call site itself
Because calling conventions are checked only at program startup, not per call
Because compilers always detect and reject calling-convention violations before producing an executable
Because this only affects debug builds, never optimized release builds
mcqs.explanation: The calling convention is the entire agreement between caller and callee about registers and stack usage, so violating it (clobbering a register the convention says is preserved) corrupts state that's only actually read later, at some unrelated point — that's exactly why these bugs are hard to trace. There's no startup-only check, compilers generally can't detect a convention violation in hand-written or inline assembly, and this affects both debug and optimized builds equally.

mcqs.question: In the traced assembly for `(a + b) * c`, register R2 is reused for both `b` and later `c`. Why is this safe?
options: R2 is a special register reserved specifically for reuse patterns
b's virtual register is dead (no longer needed) by the time c's value is loaded, so their live ranges don't overlap and sharing the physical register is safe
The compiler always reuses the second register used in any expression, regardless of live ranges
It isn't actually safe; this is a bug in the traced example
mcqs.explanation: Once ADD consumes R2's value (b), that value is never needed again, so its live range ends there — loading c into the same physical register afterward has no correctness cost since nothing overlapping depends on b anymore. There's no special reserved-register mechanism, no blanket rule about reusing "the second register," and the reuse is a correct, deliberate allocator decision, not a bug.
